reference_opening.argument: This video is scam content because a promotional OneCoin webinar urges listeners to join a mining queue, presents participation as a path to making an absolute fortune, and gives a one-year value estimate for mined coins. It adds a limited-time token-splitting benefit, urges action before mining difficulty rises, and promotes package-based recruitment while claiming that attracting more miners will raise the coin's market price. the available video evidence does not establish whether viewers paid, received tokens, or realized any stated value.

opening.argument: Judge the investment discussion by what it actually promises. The speaker describes future coin value conditionally, saying, “if the coin is valued at 2.5 euro,” and explicitly leaves the token decision to the listener. She also says she hopes for “slow and steady” development, rather than presenting a certain price trajectory. Those qualifications matter: the one-year arithmetic is an illustration, not evidence that anyone will receive that value. The pitch is optimistic, but optimism and a conditional forecast do not themselves establish a guaranteed return or a realized loss.

I hope that our development will be slow and steady and the coin development will be in a much more steady and not so many peaks and in a sustainable way

rebuttal.rebuttal: The cited package price and mining-button example show a cost and a proposed conversion, not that the illustrated future euro value was paid out or guaranteed. The speaker’s own phrasing makes valuation conditional and acknowledges that selling tokens is an available choice. Recruitment language deserves scrutiny, but the opening’s citations do not turn that conditional example into proof of a guaranteed return.

citations.quote: if the coin is valued at 2.5 euro
I would say it's your decision what you want to do with your tokens

true_side_reply.rebuttal: A conditional calculation does not neutralize the solicitation. The speaker contrasts selling tokens now with a much larger hypothetical future value and tells listeners that more entrants make the coin more valuable. Elsewhere the webinar urges people to mine immediately under a limited promotion. The concern is the paid mining and appreciation pitch itself, not a claim that payouts or losses have already been verified.

opening.argument: Much of this webinar is an operational explanation of a mining system. The speaker says she will cover how mining works “a bit on technical side,” invites a Q&A, explains where to find the mining menu, and describes how the company’s pool distributes coins. She also addresses why the displayed blockchain has few transactions. That question-driven structure supports reading the material as an explanation for existing participants trying to understand their accounts, even though some speakers favor participation. The technical answers do not, by themselves, prove that the described system produced the advertised value.

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening points to package sales and recruiting, but those excerpts omit the extended answers about mining menus, pool operation and transaction visibility. Explaining a system to participants can coexist with promotional remarks. Nor does the quoted one-year example demonstrate that its projected valuation occurred; the speaker presents that figure as conditional.

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The tutorial framing omits what participants are urged to do with that information. The speaker directs them to sign up for mining and urges immediate participation before difficulty rises. A later speaker tells them to bring packages into the business and recruit new miners to push up the coin’s value. Technical Q&A is part of this promotional presentation, not its alternative.

Yes please do so because in four weeks the mining difficulty will go up and this a limited promotion
make sure just really bring the packages inside the business

opening.argument: The described transaction has identifiable commercial terms: participants obtain tokens through packages, can put tokens into mining, and can choose to sell tokens instead. The speaker even compares the immediate sale amount with a hypothetical future coin value. That is a promotion of a risky product, but this record does not show a viewer transferring money, being denied a withdrawal, or receiving the projected return. The cited recruiting instruction asks people to bring packages into the business; it does not itself specify a commission or demonstrate that anyone earned one. A careful decision should distinguish the troubling sales claims from outcomes the video never establishes.

citations.quote: because I paid only €1.20 for this token
now should mine now or wait or should I sell my tokens
let's say I sell 12 tokens today.
make sure just really bring the packages inside the business

rebuttal.rebuttal: The opening correctly identifies a package price, mining conversion and recruitment appeal. But it moves from those statements to a conclusion about the transaction without showing an actual purchase, a completed payout or an inability to sell. The speaker discusses selling tokens as a choice, while the projected coin valuation remains conditional. Those limits should constrain what is inferred from the pitch.

citations.quote: let's say I sell 12 tokens today.
if the coin is valued at 2.5 euro

true_side_reply.rebuttal: The absence of a documented victim does not make this ordinary commerce. The webinar links paid packages to mining, urges people to act before difficulty rises, and says recruiting more miners will increase the coin’s price. Those are the mechanism and promised upside being promoted. Whether any viewer ultimately bought or withdrew tokens is a separate question that the video need not resolve to assess its solicitation.
